Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier GmbH. ValidYN="Y">10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129298</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0264-410X(26)01107-2</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Rapid antigenic evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and waning immunity have reduced antibody-mediated neutralization, enabling breakthrough infections and sustained transmission despite widespread immunity. This highlights the need for variant-adapted booster vaccines. However, pre-existing immunity may influence the magnitude and specificity of immune responses induced by variant-adapted booster vaccination. Using the Syrian hamster model, we previously described a safe and efficient mucosal vaccination approach using live attenuated viruses (LAV) based on a "One-to-Stop (OTS)" codon modification strategy. Whether OTS vaccines are suitable as effective booster vaccines in the presence of pre-existing mucosal immunity remained unaddressed. Here, we modeled pre-existing hybrid immunity in Syrian hamsters using intramuscular bivalent mRNA vaccination followed by SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequently administered heterologous intranasal OTS-LAV or intramuscular mRNA XBB.1.5 booster vaccination. Both booster strategies significantly increased XBB.1.5-binding- and neutralizing antibodies systemically and at mucosal sites. In contrast, booster vaccination left SARS-CoV-2 specific T cell frequencies unchanged. While all hybrid-immune animals were protected from disease following XBB.1.5 challenge infection, virus transmission was completely blocked only after booster vaccination and was associated with the absence of infectious virus in nasal samples. Collectively, using OTS-LAV we provide a proof of concept that intranasal LAV vaccination can effectively boost pre-existing hybrid immunity and restrict viral transmission. These findings support the use of OTS-LAV as a heterologous booster strategy against SARS-CoV-2 and demonstrate that variant-adapted booster vaccination can efficiently limit transmission, a strategy highly desired for tackling emerging respiratory infections.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026. ValidYN="Y">e20260092</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.70962/jhi.20260092</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>We previously reported that two of three patients with severe Usutu virus (USUV) disease carried circulating autoantibodies (auto-Abs) neutralizing type I IFNs (AAN-I-IFN). Here, we studied four additional patients, bringing the total number of European patients with life-threatening USUV infection to seven (Austria, n = 1; France, n = 1; Hungary, n = 4; Italy, n = 1). Three of these patients (all male, aged 43, 77, and 78 years, one French and two Hungarian) had blood auto-Abs neutralizing at least 10 ng/ml IFN-α2 and IFN-ω and at least 1 ng/ml IFN-β. They suffered from meningitis (n = 1), meningoencephalitis (n = 1), or myocarditis (n = 1). The other four patients were similar demographically and clinically but had no detectable AAN-I-IFN. No AAN-I-IFN were found in the 63 individuals with silent USUV infection tested (P = 6.4 × 10-4, Fisher's exact test). These AAN-I-IFN increased the risk of life-threatening USUV disease by 98.8-fold (95% CI: 4.12-2,369; P = 0.0046, Firth's bias-corrected logistic regression) and, thus, account for almost half the cases of life-threatening USUV infection in Europe.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© 2026 Gervais et al.</CopyrightInformation></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author Although numerous novel ADPs have recently been discovered, the mechanisms by which most act remain uncharacterised. Here, we employed computational structural approaches to predict mechanisms of action for 19 uncharacterised ADPs. Many ADPs, while inhibiting one defence system, simultaneously trigger another, and we found features shared by these proteins, and in addition revealed previously unreported links between ADPs and defence triggers. Given the extensive evolutionary links between bacterial and eukaryotic viruses, and the established homology between eukaryotic innate immune systems and bacterial defences, we hypothesised that eukaryotic viruses may encode homologues of phage ADPs and use them to evade eukaryotic immunity. We identified homologues for 20 phage ADPs in eukaryotic viruses, with nucleotidyltransferase predicted to retain analogous functions. Together, these findings shed light on the putative mechanistic diversity of phage ADPs and suggest that molecular strategies for immune evasion may be conserved across the prokaryotic and eukaryotic Its increasing association with multidrug resistance (MDR) severely constrains current therapeutic options, underlining the urgent need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. In this study, we aimed to isolate and comprehensively characterize a novel bacteriophage, ΦAB114, targeting MDR A. baumannii through morphological, biological, and genomic analyses. ΦAB114 was characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), host range analysis, and Illumina-based whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Functional genome annotation, comparative genomics, and phylogenetic analyses were performed to determine its genetic features, evolutionary relationships, and the presence of antibiotic resistance or virulence-associated genes. TEM analysis revealed that ΦAB114 exhibits a siphovirus-like morphology and belongs to the class Caudoviricetes. ΦAB114 was able to infect 20 of 72 clinical A. baumannii isolates, including carbapenem- and colistin-resistant strains WGS identified a putatively linear double-stranded DNA genome of 37,423 bp with a GC content of 39.76%, encoding 55 putative ORFs. Functional annotation revealed genes involved in structural assembly, DNA packaging, replication, and regulation, while an integrase gene suggested a temperate lifestyle. Comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses showed high sequence similarity to Acinetobacter phages Ab105-1phi and AbTJ. No antibiotic resistance or virulence-associated genes were detected. The genomic characteristics of ΦAB114, the absence of detectable antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes, and its observed activity against MDR A. baumannii clinical isolates contribute to the genomic and biological characterization of this temperate phage, underscoring the need for further experimental studies to fully evaluate its biological behavior and potential applications.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. ValidYN="Y">10.1016/j.virol.2026.111111</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0042-6822(26)00327-2</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Human G11P[25] rotaviruses reported to date have been porcine-like strains with relatively conserved Wa-like genomic backbones. A novel human G11P[25] strain, RVA/Human-wt/JPN/S22-592/2023/G11P[25] (short name, S22-592), was detected in stool from a 17-year-old boy hospitalized with severe gastroenteritis in Japan. In this study, we sequenced and characterized the whole genome of strain S22-592. Whole-genome analysis revealed a unique genotype constellation, G11-P[25]-I12-R2-C3-M3-A3-N2-T3-E1-H1. Phylogenetic analysis and sequence comparisons indicated that five of the 11 genomic segments (VP7, VP4, VP6, NSP4, and NSP5) are most similar to those of Korean porcine-like human G11P[25] CAU12-2-like strains, which possess the genotype constellation G11-P[25]-I12-R1-C1-M1-A1-N1-T1-E1-H1, representing an I12-containing Wa-like backbone. Of the remaining segments, VP1 and NSP1-NSP3 are most closely related to Chinese feline-like human G3P[9] 2020999/23582009-like strains, which have the genotype constellation G3-P[9]-I2-R2-C2-M2-A3-N2-T3-E3-H3, whereas VP2 and VP3 are most closely related to Thai/Japanese human G3P[9] B2682/To16-11-like strains, which have the genotype constellation G3-P[9]-I3-R3-C3-M3-A3-N3-T3-E3-H6. Together, these findings expand the known range of human G11P[25] rotaviruses beyond the relatively conserved porcine-like/Wa-like lineages described previously, and suggest that S22-592 represents a genomic mosaic assembled from segment groups with distinct porcine-, human-, and feline-associated evolutionary histories.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 The Authors. macrophages.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>2740247</StartPage><MedlinePgn>2740247</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">2740247</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1080/01652176.2026.2740247</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Using fluorescently labeled African Swine Fever Virus (ASFV) strains, a high (~0.2) quasi-recombinant frequency (qRF<sup>3-4</sup>) was detected <i>ex vivo</i> during 3-4 replication cycles in naïve porcine alveolar macrophages (PAM). While co-infection and recombination frequencies remained low in PAM, they increased sharply between the second and fourth viral cycles. Infection multiplicity and synchronicity significantly influenced ASFV recombination frequency, which correlated positively with genetic distance. Crossing the ASFV/Lv17/WB/Rie1 mutants yielded a saturation curve resembling the Haldane mapping function, plateauing at ~20% recombination frequency at 160 kbp. Crossing less homologous strains (ASFV/Lv17/WB/Rie1 × ASFV/NHV/P68) reduced the recombination frequency; however, at large marker distances (140 kbp), it approached values (0.18) observed in homologous strains. A novel mathematical model estimated the average co-infection rate to be 0.47 after three <i>viral</i> cycles. Empirical application of the model revealed that 1 centimorgan translates to ~550-1650 bp, meaning offspring virions from a single cell undergo an average of 1.15-3.45 recombination events. This high recombination rate is consistent with <i>in vivo</i> observations and has critical implications for ASFV prevention and vaccination strategies. Such genomic plasticity can facilitate rapid viral evolution, potentially undermining the efficacy of live-attenuated vaccines globally.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author Whether their differentiation toward effector or memory fates is stochastic or TCR-dependent has remained unclear, largely because the vast diversity of TCRs makes individual clones difficult to trace over time. Using single-cell RNA and TCR sequencing in acute LCMV Armstrong infection, we found that clonal distributions in blood reflect those in lymphoid organs, enabling nonlethal longitudinal tracking of clonal evolution. Tracing hundreds of clones, we found that memory clonal distribution is surprisingly uncoupled from early dominance; instead, early central memory precursor frequency predicts memory dominance. Leveraging convergent recombination, we identified clones with identical CDR3 amino acid sequences in mice and found that these natural biological replicates were more likely than chance to adopt similar fates, although substantial clone-to-clone variation remained. Applying the TCR distance algorithm, we further identified dominant motifs associated with enhanced expansion and effector-biased transcriptional programs, extending the TCR's role in shaping clonal divergence.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>2760125</StartPage><MedlinePgn>2760125</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">2760125</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1080/22221751.2026.2760125</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses have undergone continuous evolution since their emergence in China, but the extent of genetic and antigenic diversification among recently circulating viruses remains unclear. Here, we characterized 18 H5 viruses isolated through routine surveillance in China during 2024-2025, together with publicly available clade 2.3.4.4b H5 sequences collected since 2020. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that these isolates formed a distinct evolutionary cluster within clade 2.3.4.4b, designated the G2-derived emerging cluster (G2-EC), which emerged around mid-2024 and exhibited clear genetic divergence from previously circulating H5N1 viruses. G2-EC viruses accumulated a characteristic set of hemagglutinin amino acid substitutions, most of which were located in antigenic regions. Across the clade 2.3.4.4b H5 virus population, the estimated mean HA evolutionary rate was higher during 2024-2025 than during preceding periods. These genetic changes were accompanied by marked antigenic divergence from the Re14 vaccine strain, with 4- to 32-fold reductions in HI titres. Genomic analysis revealed acquisition of PB1 segment from a distinct genetic background in G2-EC H5N1 viruses, followed by the emergence of H5N6 viruses sharing a highly similar genetic backbone but carrying a distinct NA segment, indicating sequential reassortment. Animal experiments showed that representative G2-EC viruses retained high pathogenicity and efficient direct-contact transmission in SPF chickens, while exhibiting relatively limited lethality in mice. Collectively, these findings document a recent evolutionary transition of clade 2.3.4.4b H5 viruses in China, characterized by genetic and antigenic divergence accompanied by sequential reassortment, underscoring the need for continued genomic and antigenic surveillance.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author These sRNAs help coordinate expression of MGE-encoded virulence factors with core genome-encoded pathways. To investigate the evolution of MGE-encoded sRNAs, we queried public databases to characterize the distribution of the genes encoding PasA, PasB, PasC, PasD1, and PasD2, five prophage-encoded sRNAs discovered in enteropathogenic <i>E. coli</i>. We find that while the <i>pas</i> genes are largely restricted to pathogenic lineages of <i>Escherichia</i> and <i>Shigella</i>, they exhibit diversity in sequence, genomic distribution, and copy number across strains. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that <i>pas</i> genes were acquired independently in multiple lineages and are associated with specific <i>E. coli</i> pathovars, consistent with horizontal acquisition followed by retention and diversification. Synteny suggests a phage origin for <i>pas</i> genes, likely from Shiga-toxin encoding phages, but the genes appear to have diverged after integration into bacterial chromosomes. Comparative and structural analyses further suggest that the PasA and PasC sRNAs share a common evolutionary origin, while PasD and STnc100, another prophage-encoded sRNA, share structural elements. These findings provide further insight into the emergence, diversification, and evolutionary persistence of accessory genome-encoded sRNAs.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Published by Oxford Recent outbreaks and antimicrobial resistance show that infectious disease threats can no longer be understood through pathogen-centered models alone. This review examines why infectious diseases are becoming more complex, with emphasis on zoonotic spillover, environmental change, climate-sensitive transmission, globalization, antimicrobial resistance, viral evolution, surveillance, and preparedness. Infectious disease complexity reflects interactions among microbial adaptation, reservoir ecology, host susceptibility, human-animal contact, land-use change, climate pressure, urbanization, mobility, health care exposure, and unequal public health capacity. Case examples including Ebola disease, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), highly pathogenic avian influenza, Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), Nipah virus disease, and mpox show that containment depends on transmission biology, exposure setting, timing of infectiousness, and health system readiness. Antimicrobial resistance adds a slower but persistent crisis because resistant organisms, resistance genes, antimicrobial residues, and vulnerable hosts circulate across hospitals, communities, food systems, wastewater, and environmental reservoirs. Preparedness should move upstream of the first recognized human case. Future strategies should make ecological prevention measurable, study reservoir-host dynamics, anticipate pathogen adaptation, reduce exposure at spillover interfaces, detect silent human infection earlier, and respond rapidly through coordinated investigation. Infectious disease control in the twenty-first century will require integrated systems that connect ecological prevention, molecular insight, surveillance, health care resilience, public trust, The worldwide seroprevalence of parvovirus B19 has been assessed to be about 40-60%. It has been shown that parvoviruses can also infect new host species, adapt, and co-evolve. A comprehensive genomic surveillance is essential to gain a better insight in the adaptation, evolution, and also epidemics of parvoviruses. In the scope of the large parvovirus B19 epidemic 2023/24 following the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, we developed a rapid and convenient system to analyze parvovirus B19 genomes directly from patient samples by next-generation sequencing. We utilized this system to study the part of the unusual outbreak in Southern Germany (Central Franconia), comprising the counties Nuremberg, Fuerth, and Erlangen. This detected a certain genetic diversity within the analyzed samples and identified shared mutations in comparison to reference sequences. Here, two phylogenetically distinct groups were observed, compatible with the co-circulation of at least two B19V lineages in the region and a putative new genotype of human parvovirus B19, possibly induced by immunosuppression was identified. We established a new, quick, and convenient surveillance system for human parvovirus B19 that enables the analysis of outbreaks and monitoring of viral genetic In 2025, Guangdong, China, experienced the largest documented CHIKV outbreak in mainland China, with 23,464 reported cases across all 21 prefecture-level cities. We conducted integrated epidemiological, genomic, and phylodynamic analyses to investigate the outbreak's origins, transmission dynamics, and CHIKV lineage evolution. The Guangdong strain belongs to the East/Central/South African (ECSA) genotype, Middle African lineage (ECSA-MAL) - one of several CHIKV lineages co-circulating globally in 2025; a long internal branch separates ECSA-MAL from previously sequenced relatives, indicating substantial surveillance gaps in endemic regions. Phylodynamic analysis using a local molecular clock model estimated that the viral introduction occurred within a narrow window in early April 2025 (95% HPD: March 26-April 12), suggesting a 2.5-month period of cryptic transmission prior to detection. The prolonged silent phase aligns with vector dynamics: the Mosquito Ovitrap Index in the outbreak town of Beijiao, Foshan, stayed low in April (3.0) before surging to 9.0 through July - consistent with suppressed early transmission followed by seasonal amplification. Human migration from the two epidemic epicenters was moderately associated with the spatial distribution of cases (Spearman ρ around 0.5), while mosquito ecology may constrain spatial spread. Phylowave analysis on global circulating strains identified 33 lineage-defining mutations across 14 sublineages, concentrated in NSP3, E1 and E2. Four of these have been experimentally validated as adaptive mutations. This study demonstrates the critical need for enhanced genomic surveillance during pre-peak months and underscores the importance of monitoring adaptive mutations across diverse ecological Beyond well-recognized extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)- and carbapenemase-producing strains, colistin resistance remains a critical concern for treating severe multidrug-resistant (MDR) infections. While routine surveillance exists, the distribution and genomic epidemiology of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across interconnected reservoirs remain insufficiently characterized. Applying a One Health framework, this study investigated cross-sectoral genetic relatedness and shared AMR determinants by analysing local clinical and retail meat <i>Salmonella</i> isolates alongside a reference set of publicly available regional genomes representing human, food, animal, and environmental sectors. We report the detection of <i>mcr</i>-positive <i>S</i>. Typhimurium ST34 lineage human clinical isolates in Hong Kong, including <i>mcr-1.1</i> and <i>mcr-3.1</i>, not previously detected in our regional dataset or local genomic surveillance archives. Nanopore sequencing revealed that <i>mcr-3</i> was carried on a mosaic IncC/IncFII plasmid displaying structural features consistent with a recombinant origin involving genetic elements shared between clinical <i>Salmonella</i> and chicken-derived <i>E. coli</i> plasmid backbones. These plasmids demonstrated high <i>in vitro</i> transferability to diverse Enterobacterales, including <i>K. pneumoniae</i>, <i>Citrobacter</i> and <i>Enterobacter</i> spp. Additionally, identification of a transferable <i>bla</i><sub>NDM-5</sub>--carrying plasmid from a pork-derived isolate highlights the presence and <i>in vitro</i> mobility of clinically important carbapenenemase determinants within food-derived strains. Comparative phylogenomic analysis of 1458 <i>Salmonella</i> genomes identified mixed-source genomic clusters among major sequence types (ST19, ST34, ST155, ST40, ST17, and ST2529), indicating genomic relatedness across multiple One Health sectors. These findings support the utility of integrated One Health genomic surveillance frameworks to monitor multidrug-resistant <i>Salmonella</i> lineages.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList We investigated a 34-year-old man in Hangzhou, China, who presented with penile vesicles and a subsequent maculopapular rash in June 2026. Routine clade-specific PCR identified a Clade Ib infection; however, whole-genome sequencing of throat-swab and blister-fluid specimens revealed a putative novel Clade Ib/IIb recombinant virus. Independent DNA extraction and both metagenomic and tiled long-amplicon sequencing confirmed identical recombination regions in both specimens, with full-length amplicons covering all four major breakpoint zones. SNP-based ancestry mapping identified a Clade Ib backbone containing a central Clade IIb insertion that was interrupted by a nested Clade Ib segment. RDP analysis using seven algorithms supported two recombination events, and the inferred breakpoints were concordant with the ancestry mapping. Phylogenetic analysis assigned the Clade Ib backbone to lineage A.4.1 and the Clade IIb insertion to lineage C.1.2. The recombinant virus differed substantially from previously reported UK/India recombinants and shared no breakpoints with them, indicating an independent origin. This finding suggests that recombinants may emerge rapidly when divergent clades co-circulate and highlights the limitations of clade-specific PCR alone, underscoring the need for sustained whole-genome sequencing and genomic surveillance.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author This study investigated the ecological origins and zoonotic potential of H14 viruses in southern China. The isolates were characterised by full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis, together with assessment of avian- and human-type receptor binding, <i>in vitro</i> replication in avian, mammalian, and human cell lines, and <i>in vivo</i> pathogenicity in mice. Four H14 AIVs (one H14N6, two H14N7, and one H14N8) were isolated. We identified a novel H14 transmission network involving <i>Mareca penelope</i> and various shorebird species, indicating a multihost dispersal mechanism. Guangdong isolates formed a distinct subclade within the Eurasian lineage, closely related to Russian and Cambodian strains. The isolates (SZ3742/H14N6, ZJ3523/H14N7, SZ3536/H14N8) exhibited dual receptor-binding specificity for avian (α-2,3) and human (α-2,6) sialic acids. Strain-dependent replication in human A549 cells showed SZ3742/H14N6 peaked comparably to DF-1 cells but lower than MDCK cells, while the others had lower peak titres. All isolates replicated transiently at low titres in mouse lungs with limited pathogenicity. Molecular characterisation revealed mammalian adaptation markers and a typical HA cleavage site motif (PDKQTR↓GLF). This study presents the first evidence of H14 AIV circulation in Guangdong, emphasising the need for enhanced surveillance in the East Asian -Australasian Flyway.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList Limited cross-protection among heterologous FAdV serotypes makes molecular surveillance essential for guiding disease prevention and control. Nevertheless, serotype distribution and genetic diversity of IBH-associated FAdVs in Thailand remain limited. To address this gap, a retrospective molecular study analyzed 56 FAdV-positive chickens associated with IBH or suspected IBH that were submitted for diagnostic investigation between 2014 and 2025. A partial hexon L1-loop region was amplified, sequenced, and analyzed by phylogenetic and deduced amino-acid comparisons. The isolates were classified into three serotypes: FAdV-8b, FAdV-11, and FAdV-2. FAdV-8b was the most frequently detected serotype, accounting for 30/56 isolates (53.57%), followed by FAdV-11 with 23/56 isolates (41.07%) and FAdV-2 with 3/56 isolates (5.36%). Temporal differences in serotype distribution were observed among the sequenced diagnostic submissions. All sequences collected during 2014-2018 belonged to species D and included FAdV-2 and FAdV-11. FAdV-8b was first detected in this dataset in 2019, and it accounted for 30 of the 35 sequences obtained during 2019-2025. Phylogenetic analysis separated Thai FAdV-8b isolates into three groups and FAdV-2 isolates into two groups, while FAdV-11 isolates were highly conserved within the analyzed region. Group-associated amino-acid substitutions were mainly located in the hypervariable regions of the Hexon L1-loop, suggesting potential relevance to within-serotype antigenic variation. Overall, these findings provide updated molecular epidemiological information on IBH-associated FAdVs in Thailand and underscore the need for continued molecular surveillance to inform diagnostic strategies and vaccine selection.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026. substitution.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>2755643</StartPage><MedlinePgn>2755643</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">2755643</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1080/22221751.2026.2755643</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">After a year of quiescence, SARS-CoV-2 activity increased rapidly in Hong Kong since June 2026. We sought to characterize the genomic profile of SARS-CoV-2 driving this COVID-19 surge in Hong Kong and to examine the global dissemination of the identified circulating lineages.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">We performed SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequencing on archived respiratory specimens collected at Queen Mary Hospital, Hong Kong, between January 2025 and July 2026. Viral lineages were assigned via Nextclade. Global SARS-CoV-2 metadata downloaded from GISAID as of July 2026 were analysed to track global evolutionary trends.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Among 615 successfully sequenced strains, the XDV descendant NB.1.8.1 was the predominant lineage. Between April and July 2026, NB.1.8.1 descendants accounted for 95.6% (108/113) of sequenced strains, dominated by PQ.16.1.1 (81.5%). Spike substitutions 420N and 478T emerged rapidly. While 478T increased gradually throughout 2025, 420N emerged in April 2026 and reached 98.0% by June-July 2026. Strains harbouring 420N-478T dual substitution arose independently across distinct NB.1.8.1 lineages, accounting for 94.4% (102/108) of NB.1.8.1 descendants in Hong Kong during this period. Globally, the prevalence of NB.1.8.1 strains with 420N-478T dual substitution increased from <1% before April 2026 to 50.7% by mid-July 2026, with the highest prevalence observed in Southeast Asia and Australia.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">The 2026 COVID-19 surge in Hong Kong was driven by NB.1.8.1 descendants harbouring spike 420N and 478T substitutions. The rapid worldwide expansion of these dual-substitution lineages highlights their competitive growth advantage and underscores the need for continued global genomic surveillance.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Tsoi</LastName><ForeName>Hoi-Wah</ForeName><Initials>HW</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>State In this study, we report the co-circulation of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N6 HPAIVs associated with mortality events in Anseriformes and Charadriiformes at a coastal wintering site in Fujian Province, China. H5N1 and H5N6 viruses were identified in four species of waterfowl (Bean Goose, Eastern Spot-billed Duck, Eurasian Wigeon, and Eurasian Curlew). Phylogenetic analysis indicated that these H5N1 and H5N6 isolates were clade 2.3.4.4b strains circulating within Eurasia and lacked known mammalian adaptation markers in key proteins. The infected birds exhibited severe systemic multi-organ pathology, with the most pronounced damage observed in the lungs. H5N6 and H5N1 viruses caused lethal injury in BALB/c mice, with H5N1 leading to systemic infection. Environmental sampling also revealed the presence of H5N1 HPAIVs alongside low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) such as H3N1 and H6N1. Our findings highlight the complex and dynamic transmission patterns of H5 HPAIV in wild bird populations and the substantial threat they pose to mammals, underscoring the critical importance of sustained surveillance for high pathogenicity avian influenza in wild birds.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author Here, we longitudinally profiled the B cell receptor (BCR) repertoire of a single volunteer who received heterologous booster vaccination followed by Omicron BF.7 breakthrough infection, integrating bulk BCR sequencing with single B cell culture and antibody binding analysis. Breakthrough infection was associated with broadened serum neutralization across SARS-CoV-2 variants and related sarbecoviruses, consistent with recall of antibodies targeting conserved epitopes. Repertoire analysis revealed stage-specific remodelling, with high-affinity binding antibodies shifting from an IGHV1-46-enriched profile after vaccination to preferential representation of IGHV3-30-3 after infection. Isolated monoclonal antibodies exhibited nanomolar-to-picomolar binding affinities to diverse animal-derived sarbecovirus spikes, with broad binding commonly, but not universally, associated with CDRH3 lengths of 14-16 amino acids. Phylogenetic and sequence analyses defined divergent evolutionary trajectories for IGHV1-46 and IGHV3-30-3 lineages, highlighting candidate genetic features that warrant validation in larger cohorts. Together, these findings describe how sequential heterologous antigen exposures can reshape the humoral repertoire in one individual and generate hypotheses for future pan-sarbecovirus antibody and vaccine studies.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Qiao</LastName><ForeName>Rui</ForeName><Initials>R</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>Shanghai
